title: Entanglement Entropy of Free Fermions on Random Fractal Lattices
abstract: Random fractal lattices provide a geometrically disordered setting in which quantum correlations can be shaped by noninteger dimensionality rather than onsite randomness. We investigate the entanglement properties of noninteracting fermions on random fractal lattices generated by a stochastic growth algorithm. By varying the growth parameter and adding missing links with probability $p$, we tune the Hausdorff and spectral dimensions while keeping the system free of onsite disorder. For ground states at different fillings, we compute the bipartite entanglement entropy of subregions defined by graph distance and analyze its scaling with subsystem size. Over a broad parameter range, we find robust power-law behavior governed primarily by the Hausdorff dimension, consistent with a generalized area law and without the logarithmic enhancement familiar from Euclidean free fermions. We also study entanglement growth following a global quench from an uncorrelated checkerboard state and uncover an asymptotic scaling collapse in which the subsystem-size dependence is governed by the Hausdorff dimension, while the temporal evolution is governed by the spectral dimension. The resulting dynamics are logarithmically slow over an extended intermediate-time window. These results show that geometric randomness alone can generate both nontrivial ground-state entanglement structure and slow quantum-information spreading in free-fermion systems.
summary: The authors study the entanglement properties of noninteracting fermions on geometrically disordered random fractal lattices. They find that both ground-state and time-evolving entanglement are governed by two distinct geometric dimensions: the Hausdorff dimension ($d_H$) controls spatial scaling, while the spectral dimension ($d_s$) dictates slow logarithmic temporal dynamics. This demonstrates that geometry alone can induce complex quantum correlations.
main_problem: Investigating how entanglement properties of free fermions are shaped by geometric disorder, specifically on random fractal lattices.
main_result: The ground-state entanglement entropy scales with the Hausdorff dimension ($d_H$), while dynamic entanglement growth exhibits a characteristic logarithmic time dependence governed by the spectral dimension ($d_s$).
method: Theoretical calculation of bipartite entanglement entropy (von Neumann entropy) for noninteracting fermions, combined with numerical simulation of fractal lattice generation and analysis of scaling laws.
model_or_system: Noninteracting spinless fermions described by a tight-binding Hamiltonian on Random Fractal Lattices (RFLs). These lattices are generated via a stochastic growth algorithm, allowing tuning of geometric ($d_H$) and connectivity ($d_s$) dimensions independently of onsite disorder.
key_observables: Bipartite Entanglement Entropy ($	ext{EE}$), Hausdorff dimension ($d_H$), Spectral dimension ($d_s$), and entanglement scaling exponents.
important_parameters:
Growth parameter ($\eta$), missing link probability ($p$), filling fraction ($
u$), subsystem size ($L$), and time ($t$).
main_assumptions: The system is modeled using noninteracting spinless fermions; results are derived by averaging over an ensemble of stochastic lattice realizations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the fractal growth process, show scaling relations for dimension extraction (Volume vs. radius, $\Omega$ vs. time), and plot entanglement entropy versus subsystem size or time to confirm power-law/logarithmic scaling governed by $d_H$ and $d_s$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model on RFLs, then calculates ground-state EE scaling ($\propto r^{d_H}$), followed by analyzing dynamic entanglement growth after a global quench ($S(r, t) \propto r^{d_H-1} [\log t]^\gamma$).
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of how purely geometric constraints (fractal structure) can dictate universal scaling laws for quantum information measures like entanglement entropy in free fermionic systems, connecting geometry directly to many-body physics.
